en: Itivuttaka 75: Tikanipāta, Third Chapter Thus it was said by the Blessed One; having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it was said by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would explain the meaning of this statement. “Then listen, Ānanda, and pay close attention; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Ānanda, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a stone pillar, the person who is like a tree stump, and the person who is like a mountain peak. And how, Ānanda, is a person like a stone pillar? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is well-born on both sides, of pure descent as far back as the seventh generation of ancestors, unblemished and of pure conduct, not suspected of being born from an illicit union. But he is unlearned, ignorant, and lacks wisdom; he does not know the Dhamma taught by the Noble Ones that leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to self-awakening, and to nibbāna. He does not practice in accordance with that Dhamma. This, Ānanda, is called a person who is like a stone pillar. And how, Ānanda, is a person like a tree stump? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is well-born on both sides... [as above] ...and he is learned, wise, and possesses wisdom; he knows the Dhamma taught by the Noble Ones that leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to self-awakening, and to nibbāna. But he does not practice in accordance with that Dhamma. This, Ānanda, is called a person who is like a tree stump. And how, Ānanda, is a person like a mountain peak? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is well-born on both sides... [as above] ...and he is learned, wise, and possesses wisdom; he knows the Dhamma taught by the Noble Ones that leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to self-awakening, and to nibbāna. And he practices in accordance with that Dhamma. This, Ānanda, is called a person who is like a mountain peak. These, Ānanda, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘There are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. “Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. It is wonderful, Ānanda, that this has been well stated by me: ‘There are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, the venerable Ānanda rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. *End of the Seventy-fifth Sutta in the Third Chapter of the Section of Threes.*
The Discourse on the Unmarried.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I have heard:
"Monks, these three types of persons are found existing in the world."
Which three?
One who is like a drought, one who rains locally, and one who rains everywhere.
And how, monks, is a person like a drought?

“Here, monks, a certain person does not give anything at all—food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lamps—to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, the wayfarers, or beggars.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is like one who does not rain at all.
And how, monks, is a person like one who rains in only one place?”
"Here, monks, a certain person gives to some, but does not give to others— namely, to recluses, brahmins, the poor,
the destitute, the wayfarers, and beggars— food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lighting.
In this way, monks, a person is one who rains locally."
And how, monks, is a person one who rains everywhere?

Here, monks, a certain person gives to all—ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, the wayfarers, and beggars—food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is one who rains everywhere.
“Monks, these three persons are found existing in the world.
Thus the Blessed One spoke. With reference to this, it is said:
“Neither to ascetics nor to brahmins,
nor to the poor, the needy, or the wanderers,
does he share what he has obtained.”
Food, drink, and solid nourishment—
men call that lowest of men "equal to a drought."
To some he gives nothing,
while to others he bestows much;
him indeed they call a "partial rain-maker."
The wise people have said:
A man who speaks kindly regarding the availability of food and who is compassionate toward all living beings;
Rejoicing, he scatters [the offerings], crying out, "Give! Give!
Just as a cloud, having thundered, [pours down rain].
Having thundered, it rains;
it fills both the high ground and the low with water,
overflowing as it were with its flow.
In the same way, there is here a certain person of such a kind who,
having gathered [wealth] in accordance with the Dhamma,
Wealth acquired through exertion,
he satisfies with food and drink those mendicants who have rightly arrived.
This matter too was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The sixth [sutta].
